To ensure reliability in real-world deployments, these systems must remain robust against hardware soft errors that corrupt platform memory. Building on the proven effectiveness of activation clipping, this study constructs a preliminary safety case for classifier and detector CNNs by showing that range propagation—defined as the set of output predictions for edge inputs that lie on the decision boundary—can be contained within tight, semantically meaningful bounds suitable for human interpretation, thereby guaranteeing system safety. We confirm the practical applicability of this approach across various network architectures, image sizes, and safety-relevant properties, including the maximum permitted wrong-lane crossing distance for vehicles and the allowable temporal gap a human robot must maintain. Furthermore, we show that directional forward propagation combined with reflectional symmetry can significantly reduce computational cost without compromising the soundness of the proof. Finally, we derive loose upper bounds on local gradient growth to offer a theoretical justification for these empirical findings. The source code for all demonstrations is publicly available. This preliminary safety case can be extended to cover end-to-end safety properties and temporal constraints, and the proposed techniques are relevant for real-time safety verification and formal certification of cyber-physical systems.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) power high-stakes applications in safety-critical computer vision, including those for automated driving and human-robot interaction. It has been nearly two decades since classification accuracy became the primary metric for comparing image classifiers, yet there remains a scarcity of research on systematically proving the safety of such systems. We introduce a novel framework for safety analysis that leverages the properties of modern CNNs, specifically their layer-wise reflectional symmetry and directional forward propagation. This approach establishes a concise and rigorous foundation for certifying the safety of both classification and detection tasks, addressing various types of hardware soft errors. The methods presented are entirely practical, scalable, and generalize to any property expressible as a collection of boundary cases. While the approach is fully automated, it can also incorporate human expertise and rules to hybridize systems. The code underlying our experiments can be found at \url{https://github.com/richardson-ryan/safety-case-for-cnn-classifiers-and-detectors}.

9, Chile, particularly its capital Santiago, experienced extensive violence that resulted in the destruction of both public and private infrastructure. This study seeks to extend an epidemiological non-local model, previously effective in describing the 2005 French riots, to include the topological structure of Santiago's subway network and account for the observed spatial distribution of rioting. While the model accurately replicated the aggregated temporal progression of the disorders, it failed to reproduce the actual spatial pattern of activity in Santiago. This discrepancy is primarily due to the model's absence of a population displacement mechanism, a factor deemed essential for explaining the unrest episodes in the city. To address this, the authors propose a set of simplified differential equations representing the unrest's topological distribution across Santiago's subway system. When integrated with an advection term representing the movement of the urban population, the system successfully replicates the reported disorder patterns for October 18 and 19, 2019, although it does not apply to the events on October 20. The divergence in the October 19 and 20 scenarios is specifically linked to the distribution of food establishments in Santiago. The findings indicate that to accurately simulate unrest patterns in a given location, one must consider not only the population's topological distribution and mobility but also the available food infrastructure. These insights can facilitate the prediction of civil unrest in major cities and inform strategies for resource allocation, population displacement, and the construction of new food services to either mitigate or manage such events. The study does not address the socioeconomic root causes of the riots. Keywords: French model; topology; mobility; food establishments; prediction; mitigation. Unlike standard methods that fail to address extended operators or infinite alphabets, the proposed algorithm bypasses the conversion to equivalent automata. Instead, it employs a purely symbolic term rewriting system to resolve regular expression inequalities. The authors present a new symbolic decision procedure for containment, utilizing Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives alongside Antimirov's rewriting technique. Furthermore, they extend Brzozowski's syntactic derivative operator into two generalized versions capable of operating on representable, potentially infinite character sets. These extensions, along with their associated properties, are investigated to develop a comprehensive rewrite rule set aimed at transforming extended regular expression terms into a canonical form equivalent to a specific symbolic subexpression of the Davis-Weycker algorithm. Experimental results indicate that this proposed algorithm outperforms the classic Davis-Weycker method when applied to regular expressions converted to extended forms via compilation rules. The source code for the algorithms discussed in this study is accessible on GitHub.

This article investigates the containment problem ($\subseteq$) for extended regular expressions that support intersection and complement operators over potentially infinite character sets. A primary contribution is the generalization of the regular expression derivative operator, originally defined by Brzozowski for finite alphabets, to expressions with extended operators and infinite character sets. This generalized operator serves as the foundation for a symbolic algorithm intended to decide the containment problem. However, due to the undecidability of the problem for a specific subclass of extended expressions (a class inclusive of regular expressions with intersection), the symbolically computed regular expression derivative is not always sufficient to determine containment. To address this limitation, the paper proposes hybrid algorithms that integrate both symbolic computation and classic automata-based methods. The rules governing the application of these algorithms are defined through a comprehensive matrix format. The rules regulate the computation of regular expression derivatives, the conversion of expressions to automata, and the execution of automata containment checks. Similarly, the generalized derivative operators are ruled out in specific contexts to prevent redundant computations. The algorithms presented in this work have been implemented in Python and are available on GitHub.

. Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) leverages data from cameras and inertial sensors to determine position and orientation. Recently, deep learning-based VIO approaches have gained significant interest because they derive pose information through data-driven methods, eliminating the need for manually designed algorithms. However, current learning-based VIO systems typically depend on recurrent models to integrate multimodal data and process sensor signals, which often struggle with training difficulties and lack sufficient efficiency. We introduce a novel framework that utilizes external memory-based attention mechanisms for efficient multimodal data fusion and robust, high-frequency inertial signal processing. This approach subsumes various fusion and processing techniques as special cases, demonstrating superior performance across diverse data fusion scenarios through extensive experiments. Combined with a reliable posterior Bayesian estimation method, we have developed a novel learning-based VIO system termed FUSE-ODOM. Extensive experiments across various scenarios show that our method achieves accurate and robust pose estimation in visually challenging environments and different lighting conditions, significantly outperforming existing state-of-the-art baselines on both the KITTI and TUM RGB-D datasets. Additionally, we conducted real-world evaluations to further validate the system's accuracy and reliability. Finally, we assessed the system's performance on a mobile agent executing closed-loop tasks, verifying its capacity for precise localization and reliable task completion. Our code and models will be made publicly available to support future research in visual-inertial odometry and mobile agent localization.

Recent advancements in self-supervised depth estimation have demonstrated strong performance for monocular cameras, yet these systems still suffer from residual ambiguities and generate outputs scaled by an unknown factor. We address this by employing a network that outputs both a relative scale and a normalized depth map, where the normalized values are constrained to lie within a specific range. We demonstrate that a wide array of state-of-the-art relative scale and depth estimation techniques can be unified into an novel framework called SELF, which estimates both metrics simultaneously. This approach offers several key advantages: it produces more robust and accurate predictions by leveraging visual cues and inter-temporal constraints; it enhances visual quality by integrating self-supervision with classical geometric methods like SFM and SVO; and it enables the incorporation of additional modalities for precise sensor fusion and subsequent pose estimation. Extensive evaluations across multiple real-world datasets validate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results in relative scale estimation, visual odometry, and self-supervised monodepth estimation. Furthermore, our method proves highly effective for visual decoding tasks, such as those found in neural decoding experiments.

This Letter introduces a square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal (SHOWS) model by adapting characteristics from its parent Hamiltonians. Our findings reveal that SHOWS supports both "Fermi-arc" surface states and hinge states linking the projections of Weyl points. We successfully constructed this exotic SHOWS state theoretically and observed it experimentally in three-dimensional (3D) stacked electric circuits featuring honeycomb-kagome hybridizations and double-helix interlayer couplings. These results pave the way for achieving square-root topology within 3D solid-state systems. Figure of Merit formulas are provided to quantitatively assess the preservation of topology within the SHOWS framework.

Square-root topology has recently been explored in various theoretical and experimental platforms, typically involving the deployment of symmetry-nonlinear Hamiltonians that mimic the linear Hamiltonians of their parent systems. This Letter demonstrates that Hamiltonians exhibiting square-root topology can emerge spontaneously from linear Hamiltonians when a particular disorder is applied. Specifically, we identify that Harper-Hofstadter and Haldane models with certain linear disorders possess eigenvalues identical to those of their parent undisordered models, implying that topological edge states can appear on insulators due to these spontaneous square-root topology states. This phenomenon arises because the projection of a chaotic operator can reproduce a linear topological operator. To quantitatively evaluate square-root topology in this context, we define a Hamiltonian $H$ as having square-root topology when a subset of its eigenvalues (or a projection of $H$) matches the energy bands (or spectrum) of a topological operator $A$ linearly coupled to $H$, i.e., $[A,tH]$. This definition is generally applicable to all symmetry-topology classifications, including those relying on non-Abelian symmetries. Furthermore, we observe that the phenomenon where a chaotic operator's projection yields a linear topological operator can occur naturally in Moire superlattices. We propose exploring square-root topology under disordered conditions in these superlattices in future research.

### 1 Introduction

Tensor network (TN) algorithms have proven indispensable in both condensed matter theory and quantum many-body physics, offering powerful solutions to difficult problems in statistical mechanics, identifying ground states and their degeneracies, exploring excited states, and conducting finite-size and scale analyses—a capability particularly valuable given the influence of boundary effects and finite-size scaling. Recently, the ability to translate TN algorithms into quantum circuit formulations has emerged as a transformative development for theoretical and readout-intensive simulation tasks. The foundational work presented in this paper establishes a pathway for developing readout-efficient quantum extensions of TN methods, a critical step for fully exploiting the problem-solving potential of readout-resiliant quantum simulators, which are anticipated to become a major focus amid the rapid advancements in quantum hardware.

While previous methods have employed cell-graphs to encode cellular morphology and organization for machine learning applications, cellular data alone is insufficient to fully characterize complex tissue architectures. Among these, the Hawkes process is particularly popular due to its ability to define the probability of new events based on the process's history. This study focuses on the nonlinear Hawkes process, which effectively captures excitation and inhibition dynamics between different dimensions. Within a nonparametric Bayesian estimation framework, we derive concentration rates for the posterior distribution regarding the parameters, assuming only mild conditions on the prior and the model. Finally, a significant challenge in multivariate Hawkes process modeling is detecting a change in the intensity function's structure, or a "jump," at an unknown time. We provide consistency results for a general class of change-point detection methods applied to this scenario. The primary contributions of this research are:
1.  Consistency for the posterior distribution of parameters in a nonlinear Hawkes process, along with convergence rates for Bayesian estimators under a Kullback-Leibler risk.

3.  Consistency for a broad class of change-point detection methods in a multivariate Hawkes process where the mean function's structure changes at an unknown time.

is renowned for its ideal conservation properties, guaranteeing exact preservation of total mass, energy, and both linear and angular momentum up to machine precision when correctly implemented. This feature is crucial for computational astrophysics applications involving binary dynamics, mergers, and the accretion of compact objects like neutron stars, black holes, and white dwarfs. However, in scenarios requiring gravity, the computational cost of calculating pairwise particle interactions becomes prohibitive. Replacing Newtonian gravity with mesh-based force calculations offers a promising alternative, as these methods are significantly faster, though they typically fail to conserve linear and angular momentum. This study evaluates the viability of SPH using mesh-based gravity calculators, specifically the periodic Green's function and the multiquadric quadratic radial basis function, through ideal gas Sod shock tube simulations. The results indicate that while momentum is not strictly conserved, the overall conservation error remains small. Consequently, we conclude that this approach is viable for astrophysical problems where energy conservation is critical but accurate momentum conservation is not, with the specific choice of mesh-based calculator depending on the timescales of particle acceleration relative to evolution. This method is especially advantageous for multi-dimensional simulations involving a modest number of particles, where it could reduce computational costs by up to an order of magnitude compared to standard SPH with direct Newtonian gravity. Furthermore, the technique is applicable to advanced particle methods like Particle Mesh (PM) and Spectral Particle Methods (SPM), which rely on a single-grid Fourier or spatial spectral calculation of gravitational acceleration instead of direct particle interactions. When combined with a momentum-conserving SPH stress calculator, the PM-SPH+ scheme could achieve computational speeds up to 100 times faster than standard SPH. Similarly, incorporating SPM could yield speed increases of roughly 10 times, resulting in comparable overall performance to SPH while ensuring strict energy and angular momentum conservation. These strategies are equally relevant for particle methods designed to solve Poisson's equation for other long-range forces, such as the self-consistent field method in plasma physics or interactions mediated by the Yukawa potential. Finally, the proposed scheme is particularly valuable for multi-dimensional problems involving a few thousand particles, representing a significant improvement over the limitations of previous studies due to computational cost. Although the 1.5 algebra superficially appears to close, a detailed examination within a tractable model demonstrates that it invariably produces an invalid BRS operator that fails to be nilpotent. This deficiency clearly extends to supergravity as well. Consequently, a revised and complete set of nilpotent first-order supergravity transformations is required to accurately comprehend 3+1 dimensional supergravity. Constructing such a set appears straightforward by incorporating two additional auxiliary fields, thereby integrating the spin connection into a super-Yang-Mills multiplet. Consequently, the 1.5 order formalism should be regarded as a sophisticated but ultimately deceptive tool. This conclusion seems to generalize to any theory involving a linear connection. This paper is complemented by four references.

In 2011, Dvali and Tolley identified a specific combination of higher-curvature terms in four dimensions that causes the massless spin-2 field to decouple from interactions. This paper challenges the universality of the Dvali–Tolley (DT) theorem, which asserts this decoupling. By constructing a simple non-linear model, we show that the DT theorem relies on a superfluous field redefinition that does not preserve the unitary BRS symmetry. We explicitly derive the correct quantum-effective action that retains this symmetry and confirm the nilpotency of its BRS charge. As a significant outcome, we prove that the DT decoupling does not occur in this framework and illustrate that massless spin-2 fields can achieve asymptotic freedom. This research is connected to four references from around the year 2020.

We introduce a novel framework for optimizing the sensitivity of $\tau^+\tau^-$ antialignment to the tau electric dipole moment (EDM). This approach utilizes optimal observables to construct the most sensitive cross section and derivative measures, enabling a precise extraction of the EDM's real and imaginary components. This method is directly applicable to both existing data from BaBar, Belle, and Belle II at $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.58$ GeV, and projects sensitivities for the Future Circular Collider (FCC) and Super $B$ Factory. Our analysis for the FCC/Super $B$ Factory assumes 50 ab$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity and full $\tau$-kinematic acceptance, whereas the Belle II estimate relies on 50 ab$^{-1}$ of data and 90% $\tau$-kinematic acceptance.

Our approach identifies four distinct regimes of optimal observables based on the specific form of the total cross section. Under the most favorable assumptions, our method improves the current best limit on the EDM by a factor exceeding 10. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these optimal observables remain robust across various experimental conditions, including reduced detector acceptance, systematic shifts in center-of-mass energy, and contributions from resonances like the $\psi(4S)$.

Finally, we show that these optimal observables could constrain a broad spectrum of new physics

Furthermore, the complexity analysis of our approach reveals that, in specific scenarios, our decoder outperforms the standard Syndrome Decoder, which remains applicable for all rank-deficient symmetric errors. The complexity of our method is characterized as $O((k/n)\cdot d^\star \cdot NIDim(m,k,q))$, where $d^\star$ denotes the minimal non-zero rank distance among the rows of the syndrome matrix, and $NIDim(m,k,q)$ represents a function dependent on the matrix dimensions and the finite field size $\mathbb{F}_q$, representing the complexity of inverting a square matrix of that dimension over $\mathbb{F}_q$. We highlight that for certain code families and fields, this complexity is quadratic with respect to the error rank. Additionally, we identify several codes with parameters and complexity profiles that are of interest within cryptography. Finally, a simulation study is presented to illustrate the performance of our decoder in correcting symmetric errors with ranks as high as $n-k$. Since the observed CMB $B$-mode polarization signal is dominated by lensing deflection, improving the estimator for $r$ beyond current levels will rely on residual $B$-modes generated by cosmic variance in the lensing pattern. This paper introduces a simple, optimal algorithm to measure $r$ from the lensing-induced $B$-mode, valid in the limit of small lensing amplitudes. Validated with a realistic simulation involving a multipole cutoff at $l_c=2048$, the method demonstrates that a $r=0.01$ signal could be measured with an uncertainty of approximately $\sigma_r \sim 0.004$ using CMB data from a $10^9\,\mathrm{km^2}$ telescope array over ten years. Notably, this estimator remains effective even when signals from inflation and lensing are mixed with a known relative sign but an uncertain magnitude. Crucially, this new estimator for small $r$ values is orthogonal to existing ones, implying it functions optimally across all $r$ regimes. The findings suggest that a detector with a sensitivity of $r \sim 0.004$ is sufficient to conclude either the existence of gravitational waves or set a null result at the historical significance level, provided the instrument can handle foregrounds effectively. The code for this estimator is accessible on GitHub.

Recently, it has been shown that if the CMB anisotropy pattern stems from an arbitrary time evolution of a single scalar field, one can define a CMB spectral index without referencing specific inflationary physics. This approach remains robust against uncertainties in inflationary initial conditions and the sound horizon. If validated by upcoming high-precision CMB measurements, this single-field assumption can be tested against data to significantly reduce uncertainty in deriving the combination $r(M_{pl}H_{end})=(M_{pl}H_{end})^2{A_s\over A_s(M_{pl}H_{recomb})}$. This test remains useful for all $r$ values, including very small ones, as long as foreground contamination can be managed. Furthermore, if confirmed, the single-field scenario would allow us to determine $r$ from small-scale $B$-mode polarization, even in cases where signals from inflation and lensing interfere with an unknown relative sign.

This work serves as a combinatorial counterpart to T. Goodwillings's utilization of screw modules in 1989 to establish a homotopyopoping operation in cohomology with integer coefficients. Compressed within a few days of lecture notes, this text provides a highly accessible combinatorial framework for understanding the differential geometry of manifolds.

Categorification has proven valuable in geometry, providing combinatorial models for cohomology. Since differential forms are forms with coefficients in coefficients, we extend this combinatorial approach to differential geometry. Combinatorial differential forms with coefficients in sheaves of differential forms with coefficients in soft sheaves can model de Rham cohomology. This extension generalizes J.L. We provide a combinatorial model for differential geometry, offering a differential approach to sheaf cohomology that parallels the standard simplicial method. Furthermore, we demonstrate that differential forms on a combinatorial differential manifold can be integrated over a combinatorial differential chain, thereby generalizing M. Fasham's findings.

Combinatorial differential geometry was introduced by the authors in a series of papers and the book *Cohomology and Homotopy through Graphs and Cubical Complexes*. In this MuLE design, lobster-eye (LE) optics are strategically arranged in an array, sharing a single X-ray camera with just a few millions of microstrip detectors. This approach utilizes LEs with varying pitch dimensions to observe X-ray transients across different energy bands: a coarse pitch (e.g., 2.5 mm) captures soft X-rays around 2.5 mm focal length, while finer pitches (e.g., 0.5 mm) target harder X-rays. Because the LEs focus onto the common camera at different angles, the MuLE configuration produces a tilted, multi-color image that encodes both spatial and spectral data. We outline the fundamental principles of this concept and calculate its imaging characteristics, such as effective field of view and point spread functions. Furthermore, we propose that MuLE optics could be integrated with existing technologies to monitor transients like supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, and fast rotating magnetars (magnetar X-ray bursts) across multiple energy bands simultaneously. to explore dark matter structure formation. Specifically, we examine how velocity and density field data influence the construction of the halo mass function using cosmological $N$-body simulations. Our approach involves training a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) on the initial snapshots of a dark matter-only simulation to forecast the halo mass into which individual particles will collapse by $z=0$, within the range $10.5 < \log(M / M_{\odot}) < 14$. Our findings indicate that incorporating velocity alongside density information yields only marginal improvements when utilizing simulations based on the standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model. However, in simulations featuring modified gravity models that introduce a screening mechanism, velocity data proves essential for achieving satisfactory results. Following training on initial conditions, the CNN achieves a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 0.189 for mass predictions, compared to a lowest possible RMSE of 0.045. These outcomes demonstrate that while velocity effects are negligible in standard $\Lambda$CDM scenarios, they are critical in modified gravity frameworks where the CNN fails to converge without such data. Based on these findings, we propose that velocity field information should be included in similar machine learning applications exploring dark matter structure formation, particularly when dealing with modified gravity theories. This study, which concentrates on piano transcription, introduces a semi-supervised approach leveraging low-rank matrix factorization, specifically Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (CNMF). Within this semi-supervised framework, only one recording per individual note is necessary. Experiments on the MAPS dataset demonstrate that the proposed semi-supervised CNMF method outperforms existing state-of-the-art low-rank factorization techniques and slightly trails behind supervised deep learning state-of-the-art methods, though it does face limitations regarding generalization. Unlike low-rank factorization, which excels in handling overlapping notes and varies audio quality, deep learning models are more robust to generalization issues. To bridge this gap, we explore incorporating prior knowledge from low-rank factorization into a recurrent neural network (RNN). The resulting semi-supervised factorization-based RNN approach achieves superior results compared to both the standard RNN and the proposed semi-supervised CNMF method on the MAPS dataset. This paper further examines the model's sensitivity to hyper-parameters and confirms its effectiveness on an external benchmark, the recently released Weimar performance collection. To ensure transparency, all models and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/AmirHamedMohammadi/Transcription.

Designed with quasi-static evolutionary applications in mind, our method utilizes a custom-developed Lagrangian formulation. Unlike the standard Eulerian approach, this formulation solves force balance equations to determine the positions of fluid elements mapped to grid points. Distinct from prior literature, we do not rely on the first integral of the Euler equation, which typically lacks a general analytic solution. Instead of prescribing the spatial distribution of angular velocity or angular momentum as previous methods do, we assign specific mass, angular momentum, and entropy to each fluid element; the angular velocity and momentum distributions are subsequently derived once the positions of all elements are established. We discretize the time-independent Euler and Einstein equations using the finite-element method, resulting in a large system of nonlinear algebraic equations that we solve via our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. To validate this formulation, we have constructed both barotropic and baroclinic rotational configurations and solved three evolutionary sequences that simulate cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion as simplified toy models. These sequences illustrate how to compute and visualize the evolution of the angular velocity distribution, including the development of centrifugal bumps. Finally, we compare the angular momentum distributions obtained in this study with those reported in recent studies that employed the conventional Eulerian formulation. Our results indicate that both conserved and actively redistributed angular momentum yield similar final angular velocity distributions, characterized by bumps on both the slow and fast rotation sides of the distribution. The formulation presented in this work offers a valuable alternative to existing methods for investigating the evolution of rotating stellar structures in general relativity. The code will be made public as the W4STAR code. The W4STAR code.

We propose a new formulation for constructing equilibrium configurations of rotating stars in general relativity. By utilizing this method, one can efficiently explore the solution space to determine the distribution of the angular momentum of fluid elements, which is crucial for modeling the formation of a centrifugal bump in the angular momentum profile when solving the subsequent evolutionary problem of a supernova remnant.

Formulated as a direct solution for the Euler and Einstein equations, this method serves as a valuable complement to the conventional Eulerian approach found in recent research. This paper introduces a novel, semi-supervised approach that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to enhance extraction accuracy. Our method combines a conditional random field (CRF)-based sequence labeling technique with a loopover strategy to identify and populate fields using solely unlabeled documents. We assess the performance of our CRF-based technique on an invoice dataset, comparing results against methods utilizing only labeled or only unlabeled documents. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly surpasses methods using exclusively labeled data while remaining computationally efficient. On a track focused on utilizing unlabeled data, our method ranks second, trailing only a similar approach that employs limited additional labeled data regarding field locations. We investigate the task of extracting structured data from legal texts using a sequence-to-sequence framework. Specifically, we develop methods to parse lists of laws and court decisions into a structured format. Our evaluations on the CourtDoc dataset indicate that these extraction tasks can be solved with high precision. We also examine the impact of different layout strategies on extraction performance and how the model can be enhanced using auxiliary information. Furthermore, we gather data from various other documents to assess the method's robustness in real-world contexts. The source code for this project can be found at https://github.com/mohammadi-ali/courtdoc. The research was funded by the Intel Corporation.

Initially, we utilize a language model to generate layout representations for the target fields based on the document's content. Subsequently, we apply a sequence-to-sequence method to extract information from the text, incorporating the predicted representations into the encoder. all three categories of compact binary mergers: binary black holes (BBH), binary neutron stars (BNS), and neutron star-black hole (NSBH) systems. For events involving neutron stars, the concurrent detection of gravitational and electromagnetic radiation offers significant potential to deepen our understanding of these phenomena and investigate the equation of state of dense matter. However, achieving electromagnetic follow-up for gravitational wave (GW) events demands rapid, real-time signal detection, classification, and parameter estimation. This process is complicated by the vast disparity in the detection speeds of gravitational wave observatories compared to the speed of their associated electromagnetic follow-up methods. This paper introduces a deep learning framework designed for the classification and parameter estimation of neutron star mergers from detector data. The proposed framework demonstrates superior performance in classification accuracy and the accuracy of parameter estimation, including the estimation of the total source mass, as measured by both median absolute deviation and the coverage of the credible region. Furthermore, the framework allows for the estimation of total source mass directly from raw detector data, bypassing the need for time-consuming traditional parameter estimation techniques. Consequently, the results of the associated electromagnetic follow-up should become available almost immediately after the initial detection of the merger event. Finally, the findings from this study are expected to be beneficial for future gravitational wave astronomy research.

Recent advancements in both gravitational wave (GW) astronomy and multi-messenger astronomy have enabled the detection of electromagnetic (EM) radiation from binary neutron star (BNS) mergers following their GW detection. This detection provides critical data for research into the origin of gamma-ray bursts and allows for the determination of the equation of state of dense matter. Although machine learning has been used for source classification and parameter estimation, it has not yet been applied to the comprehensive analysis of all data from all detected GW events. This study employs a deep learning framework for the complete analysis of data from all GW sources with total redshifted mass $M_{\rm tot}Z > 0.3/M_{\odot}$, which includes all currently detected sources. The analysis involves the complete electromagnetic (EM) follow-up of BNS and NSBH mergers, as well as the estimation of total source mass for all detected events. While the proposed framework is designed for the complete analysis of all detected sources given current detector sensitivity, it is expected to remain effective even as detector sensitivity improves. The results demonstrate that the framework yields highly accurate source mass estimates for all detected events, including those from events with undetected EM radiation. However, many SDoH factors are not coded in structured formats within electronic health records (EHRs, or simply, records). Consequently, healthcare providers and patients struggle to query, aggregate, or visualize this essential information. Furthermore, existing natural language processing (NLP) techniques for medical text often assume that SDoH details are explicitly mentioned, a limitation that hinders their performance when such details are omitted, as is frequent in real-world clinical texts. This study introduces a novel pipeline designed to extract, evaluate, and redact SDoH information from records, even when it is left unmentioned. Specifically, the system aggregates SDoH data to update or enrich patient profiles and employs a custom exonym encoder to improve the privacy of extracted information. **Methods.** Our pipeline integrates a newly developed card NLP system with a probabilistic graph-based method for extracting structured data. The card NLP module utilizes large-scale pre-trained language models to assess the likelihood that a sentence mentions a specific SDoH detail, offering a potential solution for the omission of SDoH data in texts. Additionally, a general-purpose card system helps identify the relevant discussion section for each SDoH detail within a record. The graph-based component verifies the accuracy of the proposed extractions. **Results.** Experiments were conducted on a corpus of approximately 10,000 records, covering seven SDoH details across 120 categories. The system correctly extracted around 70% of the SDoH information that was actually mentioned in the texts. Additionally, we demonstrated that our card NLP module significantly outperforms traditional NLP techniques when SDoH data is omitted. **Conclusion.** Our pipeline effectively extracts SDoH details from records, addressing the challenge of their omission. It aggregates these details to enrich or update patient social history profiles and employs a custom exonym encoder to safeguard the privacy of the information. This encoder was shown to drastically reduce the risk of re-identifying individuals. The system has been deployed in a pilot program at a major US healthcare network.

We explicitly address and solve two optimal control problems: minimizing travel time and minimizing quadratic cost to move the swimmer between fixed positions using periodic control. By considering a single dynamic switch and leveraging the motion equations' structure, we decompose the problem into simpler sub-problems. Solving each sub-problem yields a discontinuous global solution, which is subsequently approximated by a sequence of continuous functions. Numerical simulations demonstrate that minimizing the number of switches is the optimal strategy for both cost functions. Furthermore, the phase portrait analysis reveals distinct regions in the control parameter space, corresponding to the behavior of the global minimum. This approach is designed to facilitate the extension of findings to multi-switch scenarios. The methods and insights presented here may also aid in addressing similar control challenges for more complex microorganisms. Finally, the specific two-link model serves as a prototype for investigating analogous problems within both parabolic and hyperbolic control frameworks. To contextualize the significance of our findings, we conclude by discussing the dynamics of a four-link swimmer.

However, pandemic-related mobility restrictions drastically curtailed these urban encounters, prompting inquiries into their broader social consequences. This study examines shifts in the frequency and geographic or demographic characteristics of urban interactions across multiple cities and restricted mobility periods during the crisis. By combining mobile data with detailed census information, we observe that while total interaction counts remained stable, the demographic and spatial diversity of these encounters declined. Specifically, the tendency for individuals to interact primarily with others from their own neighborhoods and age groups diminished, particularly in areas heavily impacted by lockdown measures. Consequently, urban dwellers de facto lived in effectively segregated communities based on income and age. Furthermore, the frequency of interactions with peers outside one's own age group and income bracket demonstrates a marked decrease under strict pandemic restrictions, a trend that could have exacerbated health and economic disparities. Ultimately, the necessity of balancing safety protocols with the preservation of urban vibrancy offers a rationale for implementing targeted, granular pandemic control strategies. Additionally, the methodology developed for quantifying these interactions across various dimensions—such as geography, demographics, and mobile networks—provides valuable insights for planning robust, interconnected urban mobile ecosystems.

At the core of the COVID-19 crisis lies a fundamental tension: the need to reduce virus transmission by limiting human contact must be balanced against the potential decline in urban vibrancy if these measures are too severe. While the impact of lockdowns on economic and mobility metrics has been extensively documented, the consequences for urban social interaction— a key driver of economic activity, community development, and innovation—remains underexplored. This paper investigates, for the first time, the impact of COVID-19 restrictions on urban social interactions as derived from Google Location History (GH) data. We introduced a framework comprising four dimensions of interactions: total count, mobility-based, demographic, and spatio-temporal dimensions. Our methodology was validated and compared against prior mobile studies through five case studies: two involving COVID-19 lockdowns in New York City (NYC) and Boston, and three examining other significant events in those same cities. Our findings indicate that while the overall number of interactions stayed relatively constant, both their demographic and spatial diversity suffered under strict lockdown conditions. This divergence between total interaction volume and their variety underscores the value of multiple interaction metrics for assessing urban vitality and the need for diverse pandemic mitigation strategies. The proposed framework can also be integrated with infection modeling to better predict epidemic outcomes. In summary, this research highlights the impact of COVID-19

We analyze the linearized stability of this flow within a Lagrangian framework, focusing on the emergence of resonances—defined as eigenvalues of the linearized Lagrangian operator that are not on the imaginary axis. Such off-imaginary-axis eigenvalues indicate a breakdown of Lin's stability theorem and suggest the potential for exponential instability, a phenomenon particularly relevant to current configurations representing moving marine vehicles. Our primary finding establishes a connection between the presence of rho-derivatives in a Bogovskii isomorphism for a current's sub-layers and the existence of these resonances. Specifically, we demonstrate that if a sub-layer fails to satisfy the rho-derivative condition, a resonance arises at a specific location in the complex velocity plane; conversely, if all sub-layers meet this condition, no resonances exist in the right half-plane, implying linear stability for smoothly translating currents. As a byproduct of this approach, we prove a localization theorem for the resolvent of the linearized Lagrangian operator. This work advances the understanding of Chierchia-Shaydukov's recent instability result for a multi-interface current with a single sign variation, offering a simplified and direct proof of their result for their particular current profile. Furthermore, our methodology yields a novel, purely Lagrangian, self-adjoint identity for the linearized operator, representing a significant improvement over the non-self-adjoint identity previously established by Chierchia-Shaydukov. The central innovation of this study is a novel normal form transformation for the Lagrangian formulation, which facilitates the identification of resonances by decoupling the system near a chloris point. This transformation relies crucially on a bi-orthogonal basis for the adjoint system near the chloris point, constructed using a "half-eigenfunction" approach for the non-self-adjoint Chierchia-Shaydukov operator.

Rainfall tracking in both time and space is essential for accurate weather forecasting, flood prevention, and water resource management. Traditional methods for measuring areal rain distribution over time rely on fixed ground-based gauges or radar. While radar offers real-time monitoring without the need for in-situ measurements, its data requires post-processing to account for terrain blockages and variations in reflectivity. This paper presents a novel approach to interpret radar data for more accurately capturing areal rain distribution. By fusing data from multiple radars or a single radar with a network of rain gauges, the method compensates for reflectivity variations and local measurement errors, thereby enhancing rain estimation in areas covered by multiple radars. Additionally, the technique can infer rain values in regions unreachable by any radar by leveraging information from surrounding gauge networks.

Introduction

Misinformation constitutes a significant global challenge. While various factors contribute to its spread, the shift in consumption habits toward social media has had a particularly profound effect. Consequently, detecting misinformation has become more difficult, making the development of robust detection techniques an urgent priority. Although existing methods offer some utility, the absence of contextual information in their design and the limited capacity of other text analysis techniques restrict their efficacy. Although contextual awareness is a recognized area of focus within deep learning, it has not yet been fully exploited for misinformation detection. This work presents a methodology that utilizes contextual information alongside other linguistic features. Specifically, we employ BERT to extract contextual representations from news snippets, news summaries, and user comments. By integrating these multi-source representations, our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on two publicly available datasets.

Our method builds upon the principles established in [4].

$\ell_1$-norm principal component analysis (L1-PCA), a robust alternative to conventional PCA, has gained significant popularity in recent years. This study examines a rotationally invariant variant of L1-PCA, which remains largely unexplored in existing literature. To address this challenge, we introduce a proximal alternating linearized minimization method incorporating nonlinear extrapolation to solve the problem's two-block reformulation. We further demonstrate that the proposed algorithm converges at least linearly to a limiting critical point of the reformulated problem, which is proven to correspond to a critical point of the original problem provided a specific step size condition is met. Finally, numerical experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets validate our theoretical findings and illustrate the effectiveness of our approach. To facilitate future research, we have made the proposed method available as an open-source package.

Outlier detection and dimensionality reduction are critical yet distinct tasks in machine learning that remain difficult to combine, particularly because standard techniques like PCA are highly sensitive to atypical data points. To address this, this paper introduces a novel, non-convex, rotationally invariant extension of L1-PCA for dimensionality reduction from $\mathbb{R}^p$ to $\mathbb{R}^k$ ($k < p$). While our approach is generally applicable, it is especially beneficial when the goal is to retain only the principal components free of outliers. Our analysis of the associated optimization problem reveals multiple stationary points, including a globally optimal solution equivalent to a truncated PCA, a sub-optimal solution representing a "outlier projection" transform, and a potentially dangerous local minimizer. We characterize these solutions using group representation theory and provide lower bounds on the number of iterations a gradient-based algorithm would require to escape this local trap as a function of $p$ and $k$. These findings offer a foundation for designing algorithms capable of achieving dimensionality reduction without being misled by local minima. Since the proposed problem exhibits a standard tight block-angular structure, a custom-made two-block convex approximation with nonlinear extrapolation can solve it efficiently. Numerical tests across various settings confirm our theoretical results and illustrate the algorithm's performance. To aid both current and future investigations into robust dimensionality reduction, the code is accessible at https://github.com/yairishai/RI-L1-PCA.

We detail the implementation of two reduction procedures and apply them to a shared test case. First, we develop a reduction technique rooted in a monolithic framework, solving both fluid and solid domains simultaneously. Subsequently, we present a second technique based on a partitioned (or segregated) method, where the fluid and solid problems are solved independently and coupled via a fixed-point iteration. The analysis utilizes a simplified benchmark derived from the Turek-Hron test case, featuring a fluid Reynolds number of 100. Numerical results demonstrate that the reduction costs for the two algorithms are comparable to those of the full-order models. Furthermore, solutions generated by the two algorithms show excellent agreement with those of the full-order models, with a maximum relative error of 7%. The relative error between the two algorithms is even lower. Finally, a convergence analysis confirms the stability of the solutions produced by both algorithms. These findings indicate that the two proposed reduction techniques are viable for addressing FSI problems. However, the current work remains experimental, and the relative error observed is not yet acceptable for real-world applications. Although the two algorithms yield stable and consistent results, optimizing their implementation remains crucial. This effort will ensure the success of the proposed reduction techniques in solving complex, real-life FSI problems. The take-home message is clear: the two reduction algorithms are functional, and their implementation can be adapted to various other settings.

In this study, we introduce a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry setup designed to measure extremely weak local magnetic fields expelled by a superconductor—acting as a "testing magnet"—via the Meissner effect. The resulting magnetic field gradient near the superconductor generates a centripetal acceleration on the atoms within the interferometer, enabling detection through atomic interference patterns. Building on the fact that gravitational acceleration of atoms has been measured with a precision of $10^{-12}$ g, the sensitivity of this method for detecting the expelled local field could potentially achieve $10^{-14}$ T. This approach offers a simple and accurate alternative to spin-precession techniques for field detection and may offer superior sensitivity for orders of magnitude below the nanotesla range. Furthermore, this experiment serves as an effective demonstration of the quantum nature of superconductivity and offers high precision for testing the completeness of this property in superconductors. The setup relies on well-established, straightforward technology. Additionally, the atomic interferometric configuration employed here is applicable to other scenarios involving local field expulsion, such as detecting Kosterl-Thouless phases in optical lattices or searching for dark matter axions using a vortex node in a superfluid. Using a tight-binding framework, we model this heterostructure by integrating exchange and Rashba fields generated via proximity to EuO, alongside temperature effects derived from Fermi statistics. Our analysis reveals that the EuO substrate induces an MCE in the 2D MoTe$_2$ layer, characterized by significant spin-polarized entropy variations at energies outside the MoTe$_2$-EuO band gap. By adjusting the chemical potential through gating, the MCE can be manipulated to achieve heating for spin-up states and cooling for spin-down states across the $K$ and $K'$ valley splitting in the valence band; conversely, both spin orientations either heat or cool within the conduction band. This survey examines three distinct proofs demonstrating CC's strong normalization property—the assurance that well-typed expressions cannot undergo infinite reduction sequences. In parallel, significant advancements have been made in applying constructive type theory to computer security. Specifically, we demonstrate how to encode Datalog programs within the Coq proof assistant to prove their total correctness. By utilizing a encoding based on relational interpretations, we achieve a linear increase in term size relative to program length. Furthermore, our constructions confirm that execution time and space complexities are linearly bounded, with the bounding functions being themselves computable in linear time. These findings represent a modest yet meaningful step toward systematically demonstrating classic computer science complexity results using methods from constructive type theory.

Additionally, we contend that the initial formulation of Martin-Löf's dependent function type contains a critical flaw, a issue that has been acknowledged by pioneers in type theory. We offer a formal counter-model that invalidates this definition within standard higher-order intuitionistic logic and present an amended definition of dependent function types suitable for use in type theories. This correction ensures the preservation of fundamental meta-theoretic properties, most notably strong normalization.

We propose learning a super-resolution network that maps images to these point measurements simultaneously. Such networks could be integrated into robotic systems like 3D object recognizers, enabling them to produce sharper, more accurate output masks.

Mask R-CNNs are now a cornerstone for visual task networks, including object detection, segmentation, and recognition. However, despite recent advances, there remains a significant gap in simultaneously detecting an object's presence and classifying its pose. While recent methods have attempted to combine detection with attribute prediction, they rely on handcrafted features and are limited to specific tasks. We present the first end-to-end approach for joint object detection and pose estimation. Specifically, we train a standard Mask R-CNN to predict both class probabilities and a specialized "pose map." This framework is entirely differentiable, offering a unified solution for any object detection target and a limitless range of pose definitions. We evaluate our method across various pose parameterizations and training configurations, establishing new state-of-the-art results for multiple detection and pose estimation benchmarks.

We introduce the PointAware approach, a novel technique for performing object detection using point-based features. Unlike traditional methods that rely on image patches centered at candidate locations, PointAware employs features derived from the image points themselves. We outline a framework for building pointaware object detectors and evaluate it across several object detection tasks. Our evaluations demonstrate that PointAware surpasses current state-of-the-art methods across multiple detection benchmarks.

While cloud tomography offers a promising method to treat clouds as fully 3D objects and has been validated for airborne data, satellite-based tomography requires more robust assessment. This study explores multiple approaches to evaluate and enhance passive satellite cloud tomography for strongly 3D clouds, using case studies of case-C and supercell clouds that exhibit robust 3D characteristics. By comparing tomographic estimates with microphysical properties derived from radar and satellite observations against the Canadian Regional Climate Model output, this research assesses tomography's performance across various cloud properties, including optical thickness and effective particle size. Results indicate that tomography performs well for clouds with moderate 3D structure but struggles when vertical optical depths exceed 20. By combining tomographic estimates with the deep cloud shadow cast by such thick structures, the effective particle size is overestimated by up to a factor of three. However, when supplemented with near-infrared (NIR) observations from the Visible Infrared Imaging Spectrometer (VIIRS), both optical thickness and effective particle size are accurately determined even for these very thick clouds, leveraging the fact that NIR observations remain sensitive to cloud thickness at optical depths up to 60. Furthermore, for clouds with moderate 3D structure, adding NIR data allows for more accurate particle size estimates when vertical optical depths surpass 10. Additionally, the study examines downstream clear air within the anvil where tomography overestimates optical depths; this is attributed to gradual droplet coalescence downstream of the updraft and the presence of a sloping cloud top. Overall, this research demonstrates that incorporating NIR observations significantly improves cloud tomographic retrievals of effective particle size for thick, strongly 3D clouds, where traditional passive satellite methods and 1D RT approximations are most prone to error. These findings support the development of cloud tomography as a robust technique for retrieving cloud microphysical properties from satellite observations, utilizing the newly available NIR data from VIIRS.

In chirped pulses, the temporal variation of frequency relative to the fundamental frequency induces a corresponding time-dependent critical density ($n_c$). We employed a chirp model that extends beyond linear approximations. Specifically, negatively (positively) chirped pulses initially interact with the target via their high (low) frequency components, followed by low (high) frequencies. Our findings indicate that the threshold plasma density required for pulse transmission is elevated for negatively chirped pulses compared to unchirped or positively chirped ones. At higher densities ($6n_c$), the improved transmission of negatively chirped pulses facilitates efficient electron heating, generating a stable, persistent longitudinal electrostatic field behind the target. This creates a potential well capable of trapping and accelerating ions. Monte-Carlo-Lorentz simulations indicate that ions are immediately expelled from the high-density region behind the target by electrons, establishing the potential well. Furthermore, we observe that the depth of this well—and consequently the ion energy—is increased by positive frequency dispersion in the plasma. We attribute the transmission differences of the chirped pulses to their localized heating effects. Regarding ion acceleration, we propose that the potential well arises from the temporary separation of plasma species due to their mass disparity, following the localized localization of energy. Additionally, we attribute the impact of frequency dispersion to the excitation of a longitudinal plasma wave. The anticipated multi-stage ion acceleration from a bifurcated sheath field suggests that chirped pulses could serve as a candidate for generating quasi-mono-energetic ion beams.

The ICM's global equilibrium is thought to be partially maintained by non-thermal pressure, particularly through the dissipation of energy via turbulent motions. However, accurately mapping this turbulence using X-ray emission lines remains difficult due to the scarcity of spatially resolved spectroscopy. Only advanced future instruments, such as the X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU) aboard the Athena mission, possess the necessary spatial and spectral resolution to quantitatively analyze ICM turbulence across all scales. Key diagnostics for these investigations include line shifts, line broadening maps, and second-order structure functions. When calculating these metrics, observations are constrained by measurement uncertainties and sample (cosmic) variance. This study extends the formalism introduced in our companion paper (Paper I) to incorporate statistical uncertainties specifically in the estimation of these line diagnostics, with a focus on structure functions. We show that statistics contribute to the total variance through various terms that depend on detector geometry, spatial binning, and the characteristics of the turbulent field, including a dependence on the scaling index $\alpha$ in the case of structure functions. We apply these formulas to estimate variance in observations from an imaginary small-scale X-IFU observation of a typical cluster like RXJ420. These applications demonstrate that, for the first time, diagnostics from a single observation could enable robust measurements of turbulent energy ($\sim$10%) and structure ($\sim$30%) even without prior knowledge of the turbulent spectrum. Furthermore, this formalism is essential for precisely determining the spatial spectrum from observations of smaller clusters and for interpreting maps of structure functions, shift, and broadening. The results from this cluster-specific application are generalized to provide formulas dependent on the spatial binning and telescope geometry, as well as the turbulent energy and scaling index. Finally, we discuss how this contributes to the objectives of the Athena mission regarding ICM turbulence. The formulas developed in Paper I and this work are applicable to the analysis of data from X-IFU, as well as from current instruments including Chandra, XMM-Newton, Hitomi, and Resolve.

Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) forms a ring-like structure. Leveraging the 870 $\mu$m continuum map from the APEX Telescope Large Area Survey of the Galaxy (ATLASGAL), we investigated the gas density structure's anisotropy within the CMZ by employing the 2D correlation function. To measure spatial anisotropy, we established the critical angle $\theta_{\rm half}$ and the anisotropy parameter $A\equiv \frac{\pi}{4\theta_{\rm half}}-1$. Our findings indicate that the density structure exhibits strong anisotropy at large scales (~ 100 pc), with the degree of anisotropy diminishing as the scale decreases. At approximately 10 pc, the structure remains mildly anisotropic. This analysis offers a quantitative characterization of the CMZ's anisotropic gas density structure, and the developed formalism is applicable to various regions for comparative studies. The methodology can be utilized to examine the anisotropy of other structures within the CMZ or distinct components, such as different mass intervals or velocity components. We contend that this approach offers a straightforward and quantitative method for assessing the anisotropy of the multi-phase structure across diverse velocity components and the center of our galaxy, facilitating a better understanding of the center's dynamics. Furthermore, this formalism is particularly valuable for analyzing the small-scale anisotropy accessible through future sub-millimeter observations from the Combined Array for Sub-millimeter Astronomy (CASA). This study utilizes QED particle-in-cell simulations that incorporate electron-positron spin and photon polarization to examine a standard laser-solid configuration where an ultraintense linearly polarized laser strikes a foil target featuring a micrometer-scale preplasma. Our results indicate that when laser intensity surpasses $10^{24}~\rm W/\rm cm^2$ and positron yield becomes significant, the produced positrons exhibit clear polarization. Specifically, these polarized positrons can achieve a polarization degree exceeding 30% and a charge greater than 30 nC, with a flux of $10^{12}\,{\rm sr}^{-1}$. The degree of polarization varies with deflection angles, reaching up to 60% at specific energies and angles. This angular dependence stems from the asymmetrical laser fields experienced by positrons within the skin layer of the overdense plasma, where radiative spin-flip and radiation reaction are critical factors. Furthermore, this positron polarization is robust and is expected to occur in future 100-PW-class laser-solid experiments, offering diverse application possibilities. In particular, these polarized positrons could enable the creation of a coherent positronium beam through laser-matter interaction, potentially facilitating the search for a permanent electric dipole moment in non-compound particles. Finally, the findings offer guidance for the design of experimental setups aimed at producing dense, high-energy, and polarized positrons using 100-PW-class laser-solid platforms.

The sensor's front-end utilizes a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to transform local temperature into two biasing currents, which subsequently determine two oscillation frequencies. While it has been analytically shown that purely toroidal or purely poloidal fields inevitably develop instabilities, numerical simulations confirm that roughly axisymmetric configurations within stably stratified stars can remain stable. Its utility depends on deriving flow equations that track the evolution of the quantum effective action as a coarse-graining parameter varies. This study details a new strategy for solving these equations by leveraging the fact that renormalization group (RG) equations can be reformulated to mirror fluid dynamics conservation laws. This analogy enables two main advancements: first, it permits the use of robust numerical methods from fluid dynamics to solve RG equations, ensuring reliable handling of nonanalytic behaviors in the effective action's flow, such as those arising from spontaneous symmetry breaking. Second, the fluid dynamics parallel offers fresh perspectives on interpreting RG flows and their inherent irreversibility. We demonstrate this connection using zero-dimensional quantum field theory models, with a discussion of extending it to higher dimensions. These results are general and applicable to both quantum field theories and statistical field theories.

In quantum field theory, effective field theories (EFTs) are typically defined by theories with an energy scale $\Lambda$ below which quantum fluctuations are integrated out. However, a fundamental question remains: can we systematically explore how the theory changes with $\Lambda$? We show that this problem maps directly onto a fluid-dynamical framework, specifically incompressible flow with a time variable $t \sim \ln\Lambda$. This allows us to employ a wide range of established fluid-dynamical techniques to investigate RG flows. As a primary application, we employ the Lagrangian formulation of these fluids to analyze phase transitions, highlighting the role of singular behaviors in the theory. Furthermore, we establish that this approach remains valid even when the field theory possesses a nontrivial kinetic term. This analogy provides a comprehensive and robust framework for understanding renormalization group flows in field theories, offering insights into phenomena like phase transitions and ensuring reliability in studying theories with nontrivial kinetic terms.

This finding aligns with other recent studies suggesting core masses in Cygnus X are generally higher than historically believed. While gravitational collapse alone may be insufficient to account for these masses, the data can be explained if cores forming in molecular clouds with metal-enriched, cool interiors have their mass estimates inflated by gas trapped in icy dust shells at 1.3 mm. Furthermore, a statistical correlation was identified between core mass and infrared source luminosity; because low-mass cores exhibit weak central heating, a significant population of low-luminosity cores is likely missed at wavelengths beyond 1.3 mm. Finally, comparing the dust-to-gas ratio to that found in solar neighborhood cores indicates a factor of five enrichment in Cygnus X. This enrichment is inconsistent with a uniform mix of cosmic abundances and instead supports a model where metal-rich ionic gas condenses onto dust grains, forming a shell that contributes to the elevated mass estimates when probed at certain millimeter wavelengths. This mechanism can account for a core mass distribution peaking at approximately $3 M_{\odot}$, which is sufficient to form an intermediate mass black hole. Additionally, these shells may manifest as radio-emitting features near a central point source. Consequently, millimeter core mass measurements provide a viable framework for generating black holes with masses ranging from a few to several $M_{\odot}$ without requiring a distinct physics process to establish an lower mass limit. The analysis also contrasts these results with models involving magnetic fields.

-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major unsolved challenge in high-energy astrophysics. A promising strategy to address this mystery involves correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos, as neutrinos directly trace hadronic interactions and remain unaffected by magnetic deflection. This paper outlines three distinct methods for correlating the arrival directions of these particles. The first, a standard transverse-impact parameter analysis, demands near 100% reconstruction efficiency for UHECRs. The second, a maximum-likelihood approach, benefits from a reduced impact parameter but requires a future detector capable of identifying UHECRs and neutrinos from the same events. The third, a novel technique, links a UHECR's energy deposition to neutrino flux after converting the neutrino signal into UHECR candidates via hadronic interactions. This third method offers two key advantages: it is background background-free because UHECRs cannot be misidentified as neutrinos, and it avoids the need for precise UHECR reconstruction beyond their energy. Additionally, it can be applied to historical data collected before the 2021 Telescopic Array neutrino limit. Despite current reconstruction issues within the Array, this new method could potentially yield a significant correlation signal. Final results will be presented at the 38th International Cosmic Ray Conference.

Contextualizing the high-energy cosmic ray spectrum requires pinpointing specific sources and their individual spectra. Recently, it has been shown that the spectral index of the cosmic ray population at Earth differs from that of their sources at high energies. This work derives an analytical formula for the energy spectrum observed at Earth given a set of sources with known spectra and redshift distributions. This formula relies on three parameters: redshift density ($q$), redshift anisotropy ($a$), and transverse-impact parameter ($b$). Our stress data aligns with established models for the slippage and anchored regimes, while we introduce a leverage rule to characterize stresses during stick-slip events. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for flow dynamics in multiphase systems dominated by strong interfacial tensions.
Interfacial roughness can trigger slippage in fluid flows. This study examines slippage in a specific system: the flow of a two-dimensional monodispersed foamy liquid, characterized by a 2D packing of bubbles, against solid boundaries. Through visual observations and stress measurements across diverse rough surfaces, we identify three friction regimes: slippage, stick-slip, and anchored films. We quantify slippage lengths and velocities using both classical models and a new roughness-based model. Additionally, we present a velocity profile model for the slippage regime derived from stress considerations and validate it against stick-slip data via a rescaling law. The transition from stick-slip to slippage is governed by a roughness factor, which is derived from the geometry of the contact line hysteresis.
We observe that contact line hysteresis on rough surfaces leads to slippage in dry liquid foams. Slippage lengths are governed by a roughness factor, verified through stress analysis and a newly developed roughness-dependent model. In this framework, slippage length varies with foam viscosity, whereas slippage velocity remains independent of it; both are scaled appropriately by inertial stress. Slippage velocities are also explained by a leverage rule applicable to rough moving boundaries. The shift from a slippage-dominated regime to a stick-slip regime occurs as the roughness factor increases.

an elastic membrane dividing two fluids of differing densities under external pressure within a rotating Hele-Shaw cell. We analyze both inextensible and highly extensible membranes, detailing the influence of membrane tension in each scenario. When the inner fluid is denser than the outer fluid, both systems display a centrifugally induced Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability that competes with restoring forces from curvature and tension, ultimately determining the finger scale. Numerical continuation methods are employed to calculate strongly nonlinear finger profiles, revealing the comparison between competitive restoring forces and the resulting finger scales. For both inextensible and highly extensible membranes, we observe a competition between a square-like mode and a circular droplet mode, with the latter emerging from a bifurcation of the former. In the inextensible case, this transition is supercritical, whereas it is subcritical for the highly extensible membrane, accompanied by large-amplitude oscillations of the fluid-liquid interface. These extended numerical simulations are validated against a boundary integral method that incorporates membrane elasticity via an energy minimization approach. Additionally, we investigate the membrane dynamics in a non-rotating frame where a pressure difference drives the system, focusing on the case where the larger pressure difference is on the side with more curved regions (lower effective potential). In this setup, elasticity creates local pressure barriers, causing the membrane to finger in reverse relative to the external pressure difference. This phenomenon is linked to a snap-through instability involving the exchange of the two pressure barriers located on the curved regions of the membrane. This -shaped configuration is further destabilized, leading to a multi-branched solution space with a complex array of bifurcations. The interplay between membrane extensibility and inertia generates a multi-fingered pattern, which we explain through a model involving competing length scales. Finally, we briefly address the case where the higher external pressure is applied to the side with the more curved membrane regions.

In these scenarios, the count of equilibrium microstates correspondss to macrostates defined by volume and entropy. In contrast, most other thermodynamic transformations occur between states characterized by a full set of intensive variables, where microstate counts do not inherently exist. Furthermore, previous formulations relied on prior assumptions regarding microstate counts during entropy-carrying processes to derive expressions for non-equilibrium microstate counts based on intensive variables; these underlying hypotheses are examined and critiqued. Based on this analysis, we propose that during an isometric process, the number of non-equilibrium microstates factorizes into a product involving the equilibrium microstate count at the current volume and a time-dependent component representing the deviation from equilibrium. To facilitate this, we introduce an isotropic microstate current that drives the factorization. The non-conservative nature of this current arises from a dissipative microstate current, which is determined by a dimensionless parameter characterizing the process. This parameter is found to depend on a dot product of the entropy production rate and a specific vector field that characterizes the thermodynamic state; it varies continuously from 0 (indicating reversible conditions) to 1 (indicating fully stationary states). Consequently, the microstate count at any point along a non-equilibrium isometric path is fully specified by a single, process-dependent dimensionless quantity that also ranges from 0 to 1. Notably, in the limit of an infinitely slow (quasi-static) expansion or contraction, the count of microstates becomes a product of two functions, each dependent solely on the volume at the respective endpoints. This outcome aligns with the well-established fact that an infinite number of intermediate states are accessed during such quasi-static volume changes. Additionally, we observe that for an ideal gas, the count of microstates during an isometric process remains constant and independent of whether the process is reversible or not; this specific behavior is not universally applicable to all substances. Finally, to ensure consistency with the first law of thermodynamics, we establish a relationship between the two dimensionless parameters governing the processes. This dimensionless parameter controls the extent to which heat transport during an isometric process is attributed to the two components of the microstate count. We demonstrate that for a general class of processes, heat transport is entirely ascribed to the component of the microstate count that changes with entropy.
